The user chose to make a graduation cap cake for the cousin's son's college graduation celebration. The planned decoration is a buttercream mortarboard and tassel; the user has never worked with fondant and prefers to use buttercream.
The user planned to add a small amount of corn syrup to the buttercream, refrigerate it ahead of time, and re-whip it before decorating the graduation cap cake.

The assistant recommended classic American buttercream made with 2 cups (4 sticks) room-temperature unsalted butter, 4 cups sifted powdered sugar, 1/2 teaspoon salt, 2–4 tablespoons whole milk or heavy cream, and optionally 1 teaspoon vanilla extract. The method is to beat the butter until fluffy, gradually beat in powdered sugar, add salt and optional vanilla, then add milk or cream to reach a smooth, spreadable consistency. The assistant suggested starting with 1–2 tablespoons of corn syrup per 2 cups of buttercream.

The assistant advised storing buttercream in an airtight container in the refrigerator below 40°F (4°C) for up to 2 weeks, then bringing it to room temperature and re-whipping before use. It also said frozen buttercream can keep 3–4 months, though it recommended refrigeration rather than freezing corn-syrup-enriched buttercream because the corn syrup might crystallize.

In the contract discussed in the judgment excerpt, clause 27, headed “Final Certificate,” states at clause 27.1 that, unless the contract says otherwise, the builder is not required to obtain a certificate of occupancy or final inspection certificate relating to the building works.

Clause 29 of the contract sets a defects liability period of 26 weeks from and including practical completion; the standard 13-week period was struck through and replaced with 26 weeks, with the amendment initialled. Under clauses 29.2–29.3, the owner may notify the builder of defects appearing after practical completion before the period ends, and the builder must rectify defects for which the builder is responsible if notified during that period.

Clause 14 of Schedule 1 incorporates Tender No. 2277, dated 22 January 2009, into the contract. The tender price included Council Development Application and Inspection Fees but did not include provision of a Final Occupation Certificate (FOC). The tender listed owners’ pre-occupation-certificate work as items 18, 19 and 20, concerning lighting and installation of indoor and outdoor clothes lines.

The appeal court concluded that the Tribunal misinterpreted the contract by finding that the builder was responsible for obtaining the Final Occupation Certificate (FOC) as part of the works, and that the works were incomplete until the FOC was provided. Clause 27 expressly said the builder was not required to obtain the certificate, and neither the rest of the contract nor the tender imposed that responsibility, notwithstanding Item 11 of Schedule 1.

The appeal court reasoned that a Final Occupation Certificate certifies that completed building works are suitable for occupation or use; it is not itself a building or planning approval, nor part of the physical building works. The court noted that the owners had to undertake certain work before an occupation certificate could be issued, so the building works handed over to the owners could not include provision of the FOC.

The appeal court held that the Tribunal erred in treating receipt of the Final Occupation Certificate as the date of completion for the purposes of section 3B(1) of the HB Act. Under the contract, practical completion occurs when building works are complete apart from minor omissions or defects that do not prevent reasonable use for their usual purpose; receipt of the FOC is not necessary for that practical completion.

The appeal court concluded that the Tribunal erred in finding that the parties entered into a new contract supported by consideration and in interpreting the contract to make the FOC issue date the completion date. Grounds 4 and 5 were not established; it was unnecessary to consider Grounds 2, 3 and 7. The appeal was allowed, the Tribunal’s orders were set aside, and the matter was remitted to the Tribunal to determine damages for breach of the 2009 contract. The owners were ordered to pay the builder’s appeal costs, to be assessed if not agreed.
